design_detail: Pooled analysis of individual participant data from eight Swedish prospective cohorts (the Swedish Collaboration on Health Effects of Snus Use), recruited 1978 to 2010 and followed to 2004 to 2013 through the national cause-of-death register. Men only, and only men who had never regularly smoked cigarettes: 169,103 men, 2,857,312 person-years, 10,928 deaths. Exposure was snus use reported once, at baseline; the comparison group was men who reported no tobacco use. Gamma-distributed shared-frailty survival models (random effect by cohort) with attained age as the time scale, adjusted for body mass index. Not a systematic review: the cohorts are those of the collaborating investigators.
can_establish: Whether, among Swedish men who had never regularly smoked cigarettes, men who reported using snus and no other tobacco at baseline died more often during follow-up than men who reported no tobacco use, after adjustment for age and body mass index, and how far that ratio moves across six sensitivity analyses.
cannot_establish: That snus itself causes the extra deaths (use reported once, main model adjusted for age and body mass index only, no pre-snus health measures, likely residual confounding by alcohol, education, physical activity and diet); absolute risks in each group (no group-specific rates are printed); anything about women, about people who smoke or smoked, about other smokeless products, pouches or vapes; or how snus compares with smoking (people who had ever regularly smoked cigarettes were excluded by design).

sample.recruitment: Eight Swedish cohorts recruited between 1978 and 2010: the Construction Worker Cohort (all workers in the construction industry, 279,897 men before exclusions, recruited 1978 to 1993), the Malmo Diet and Cancer Study, the northern Sweden MONICA study, the National March Cohort (participants in a charity walk), the Scania Public Health Cohort, the Screening Across the Lifespan Twin study (SALT), the Stockholm Public Health Cohort and the WOLF employee study. Seven collected tobacco use by self-administered questionnaire and one (SALT) by structured telephone interview (Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 4th paragraph; Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men only (the authors say snus use is rare in women). Excluded from the 383,015 men in the cohorts: ever regular cigarette use (n = 202,171), age under 18 (6,697), missing body mass index (1,901) and missing tobacco information (3,143), leaving 169,103 (Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). The analysed groups are men who never used tobacco, men who currently use snus and nothing else, and men who formerly used snus and nothing else.
sample.demographics: Mean age at entry 36 years (range 18 to 99): 29 (SD 11) in the current snus group, 38 (SD 16) in the never-used-tobacco group and 38 (SD 13) in the former snus group. Mean body mass index 24.1 to 25.0. In the current snus group 37.9% were in the highest alcohol tertile against 20.2% of the never-used-tobacco group, and 52.6% had 10 to 12 years of education against 38.7% (Table 2). Ethnicity, income and occupation are not reported beyond the cohort descriptions.
sample.attrition: Follow-up was by linkage to national registers; losses to follow-up (emigration, for example) are not described. Mean follow-up was about 17 years per man (editors' calculation: 2,857,312 person-years divided by 169,103). Cohort follow-up ended between 2004 and 2013 (Table 1).
sample.selection_effects: The cohorts are those of the collaborating investigators, not a systematic selection, and the text calls all eight population-based although Table 1 lists an occupational cohort, a charity-walk sample, an employee study and a twin register. One cohort dominates: leaving out the Construction Worker Cohort removes 87% of the deaths in the current snus group (1,233 of 1,410) and 66% of those in the never-used-tobacco group (6,116 of 9,272) (editors' arithmetic from Tables 3 and 4). Excluding everyone who had ever regularly smoked cigarettes leaves a younger group (the current snus group averaged 29 years) who are mostly followed from early adult life; men who smoked and then switched are not in the analysis. Because the men were already using snus at baseline (prevalent use, not new use), any earlier harm that removed some of them before baseline cannot be seen (editors' point).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported current snus use at baseline in all eight cohorts, former use in six, weekly amount in six and duration in five (Table 1). Use was not updated during follow-up and was not checked against a biomarker. In the two cohorts without data on former use (Malmo and Scania), men who did not currently use snus were classed as never having used it, so the reference group there includes some former snus use (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported at baseline among men who currently use snus only. Amount in cans per week: under 4, 4 to 6, 7 or more. Duration: under 5, 5 to 9, 10 to 14, 15 or more years. Route: oral (snus is placed under the lip, Introduction, 1st paragraph). Brand, nicotine content and nitrosamine content of the snus were not recorded.
exposure.polysubstance: Everyone who had ever regularly smoked cigarettes was excluded, so the comparison is snus-only against no tobacco. Smoking started after baseline is not tracked, and any use of cigars, pipes or other nicotine products in the reference group is not described. Alcohol intake is higher in the current snus group (Table 2) and was adjusted for only in a subset analysis.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Men who formerly used snus (5,691; 4.8% of men in cohorts that recorded former use) were analysed as a separate group, with no information on when they stopped.

comparison.controls: Men who reported never using tobacco (n = 124,256; 73.5% of the sample).
comparison.matching: No matching. All models used attained age as the time scale and adjusted for body mass index. A sensitivity analysis in the six cohorts with the information (leaving out the Construction Worker Cohort and the Malmo study) added education, alcohol and physical activity; another added calendar year (Methods › Sensitivity analyses).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Beyond body mass index, no baseline health measures are used (no prior disease, blood pressure, blood lipids, mental health, diet, income); the cohorts' own baseline data were not harmonised for these. Snus use before baseline is not related to health before baseline, and smoking taken up after baseline is not tracked.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Alcohol was available in seven cohorts (all but the Construction Worker Cohort) as tertiles of grams per week; the snus group drank more (Table 2). Cigarette smoking was excluded by design at baseline; later smoking is unmeasured.

outcomes.instruments: Deaths from the Swedish National Cause of Death Register, coded to ICD-9 and ICD-10: all causes; cardiovascular disease (ICD-9 390 to 459, ICD-10 I00 to I99); cancer (ICD-9 140 to 208, ICD-10 C00 to C97); 'other causes' (every other death, for example respiratory disease, infection, accident, suicide) (Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Register-based death and cause coding, with a published validation of death certification cited. Cause of death was missing for part of the deaths: the cause-specific counts in Table 3 add to 9,722 of 10,928 deaths, so 1,206 (11%) have no classified cause (editors' arithmetic), although the Methods define 'other causes' as every death not coded cardiovascular or cancer.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is death during follow-up, expressed as a hazard ratio against men who never used tobacco. No non-fatal outcome, no cause-level detail within 'other causes' (for example suicide, accidents or respiratory disease) and no absolute risk is reported.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four mortality outcomes; Table 3 holds 40 hazard ratios and Table 4 another 24. The text does not designate a single primary estimate; all-cause mortality for current against never use leads the abstract.

analysis.effect_sizes: Adjusted hazard ratios (aHR, adjusted for attained age and body mass index), current snus-only group against never used tobacco (Table 3): all causes 1.28 (95% CI 1.20 to 1.35; 1,410 deaths against 9,272); cardiovascular disease 1.27 (1.15 to 1.41; 443 against 3,444); cancer 1.12 (1.00 to 1.26; 332 against 2,660); other causes 1.37 (1.24 to 1.52; 511 against 2,098). Former snus-only group: all causes 1.15 (1.02 to 1.31); cardiovascular 1.13 (0.91 to 1.41); cancer 1.26 (1.01 to 1.57); other causes 1.14 (0.89 to 1.45). By weekly amount in the current group, all causes: under 4 cans 1.28 (1.16 to 1.41), 4 to 6 cans 1.17 (1.06 to 1.29), 7 or more 1.37 (1.25 to 1.50), p for trend 0.09; cardiovascular 1.44, 1.18, 1.17, p for trend 0.03; cancer 1.13, 1.17, 1.01, p for trend 0.22; other causes 1.24, 1.18, 1.65, p for trend 0.001. By duration, all causes: under 5 years 1.08 (0.88 to 1.32), 5 to 9 years 1.17 (1.00 to 1.36), 10 to 14 years 1.31 (1.12 to 1.52), 15 or more years 1.29 (1.20 to 1.38), p for trend 0.001; cardiovascular 0.98, 0.99, 1.16, 1.32, p for trend 0.001; cancer 0.68, 0.94, 1.08, 1.12, p for trend 0.11; other causes 1.13, 1.21, 1.46, 1.49, p for trend 0.001. Sensitivity analyses (Table 4, current against never, all causes / cardiovascular / cancer / other causes): leaving out the Construction Worker Cohort 1.42 (1.21 to 1.66) / 1.39 (1.05 to 1.84) / 1.52 (1.15 to 1.99) / 1.34 (0.97 to 1.86); follow-up capped at 10 years 1.34 (1.21 to 1.48) / 1.13 (0.93 to 1.38) / 1.24 (1.02 to 1.52) / 1.57 (1.35 to 1.83); extra adjustment for education, alcohol and physical activity (two cohorts left out) 1.46 (1.22 to 1.75) / 1.56 (1.14 to 2.14) / 1.51 (1.12 to 2.03) / 1.20 (0.83 to 1.72); the other three analyses (first-year events removed, cohorts without former-use data removed, calendar year added) left the all-cause ratio at 1.28 and moved the cause-specific ratios by 0.00 to 0.03.
analysis.covariates: Attained age (as the time scale) and body mass index in every model. Education (three levels), alcohol (four levels) and physical activity (four levels) only in a sensitivity analysis restricted to six cohorts; calendar year in another. Smoking, diet, income and baseline disease were not adjusted for (smoking by exclusion at baseline only).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned in the article read.
analysis.selective_reporting: All six sensitivity analyses named in the Methods are reported, including the one that removes the statistical significance of the cardiovascular result (10-year follow-up). Gaps: the proportional-hazards test is named but its result is not printed; no results by cohort are shown, although one cohort supplies most deaths; no absolute rates by group.
analysis.power: Large for all-cause mortality (10,928 deaths) but thin in places: 13 cardiovascular deaths in the under-5-years group, and 158 deaths in the current snus group in the fully adjusted subset (Tables 3 and 4), so those intervals are wide.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among Swedish men who had never regularly smoked cigarettes, men who reported using snus and no other tobacco at baseline had 1.28 times the hazard of death from any cause over about 17 years of follow-up (1.20 to 1.35) compared with men who reported no tobacco, adjusted for age and body mass index only. The ratios were 1.27 for cardiovascular deaths, 1.37 for other causes and 1.12 for cancer (lower limit 1.00). The all-cause ratio rose with years of use (1.08 for under 5 years to 1.29 for 15 or more) but not clearly with weekly amount. The cardiovascular ratio fell to 1.13 (0.93 to 1.38) when follow-up was capped at 10 years, and the cancer ratio was higher (1.52) after leaving out the largest cohort. Men who formerly used snus also had a raised all-cause ratio (1.15).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that snus use among men is associated with higher all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, deaths from other causes and possibly cancer mortality, and the paper says 'if causal' for its public-health reading. Gaps: (1) the abstract and Key Messages do not carry the Discussion's own caution that the cardiovascular result is inconsistent across analyses and should be interpreted with caution (Discussion, 3rd paragraph); (2) the abstract says risks rose with duration but not with weekly amount, whereas Table 3 shows a significant trend by amount for cardiovascular deaths that runs the other way (1.44 under 4 cans, 1.17 at 7 or more; p for trend 0.03) and for other-cause deaths (p for trend 0.001), and the Discussion (6th paragraph) itself reports dose-response trends for other-cause deaths by both amount and duration; (3) the cancer ratio did not rise with duration (p for trend 0.11), which the Results text acknowledges but the abstract does not; (4) the Key Messages say the findings may help understand other non-smoked nicotine products such as e-cigarettes, which these data cannot show; (5) the Discussion's explanations for the excess of other-cause deaths (alcohol, self-harm, violence, risk-taking) are untested hypotheses, as no cause-level data are shown; (6) the Key Messages say associations were 'systematically' examined, but the cohorts were not systematically selected.

timeline.event: Bolinder et al. followed the Construction Worker Cohort for 12 years and reported about 40% higher overall mortality in men using snus only (odds ratio 1.4, 1.3 to 1.8), as cited in this paper. That cohort is also inside the pooled analysis, so the two are not independent.
Roosaar et al., a separate Swedish cohort, reported an odds ratio of 1.23 (1.09 to 1.40) for mortality in men who had ever used snus (current and former not separated), as cited in this paper.

Hansson et al., pooled analysis from the same collaboration (eight cohorts): no link with new heart attacks but higher short-term fatality, as described in this paper; a 2014 pooled analysis on stroke is described the same way.
Lee's updated review of epidemiological evidence on snus and health (appraised in this batch).
This pooled analysis: all-cause hazard ratio 1.28 for exclusive current snus use against no tobacco in 169,103 never-smoking Swedish men.
Systematic review of cancer risk among men and women using Swedish snus exclusively, against no tobacco (appraised in this batch).

replication.where_it_stands: The largest single analysis of snus and mortality found, and consistent in direction with two earlier Swedish reports (one of them drawing on the same construction-worker cohort). All the evidence it adds comes from Swedish men, mostly followed from early adulthood, with use measured once. Whether the excess is due to snus, to the people who choose it or to later smoking is not settled by this study; the authors themselves call for caution on causation.

funding.funder: Department of Public Health Sciences, Karolinska Institutet; Region Vasterbotten; Region Vasternorrland; the Joint Committee of County Councils in Northern Sweden (Visare Norr); the regional agreement between Umea University and Region Vasterbotten (ALF); the Swedish Society of Medicine. The paper states the funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit.
funding.affiliations_note: The principal investigator of each contributing cohort provided the individual participant data (Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 1st paragraph), and the authors include those investigators; they are also authors of earlier snus reports from these cohorts. No tobacco, vape or pharmaceutical industry funding or tie is declared. The affiliations themselves were not in the page text read.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that records snus, cigarette and other nicotine use repeatedly through follow-up (so later smoking and stopping are counted), measures baseline health, alcohol, diet, income and physical activity in everyone, includes women, reports absolute death rates by group and by cause, and compares snus-only with people using nicotine replacement and with people who stopped all nicotine, so that the nicotine and non-nicotine parts of snus can be told apart. A randomised trial is not feasible for mortality.

domains.note: The main model adjusts for attained age and body mass index only. Men in the snus group drank more and had less education (Table 2), and diet, income, baseline illness and later smoking are unmeasured. The adjusted subset analysis (education, alcohol, physical activity) gave similar or larger ratios (1.46 against 1.42 when only the largest cohort was left out) but covers 11% of the snus-group deaths and still leaves other confounders, so confounding cannot be ruled out.

Self-reported at baseline, once, with no biomarker; former use unrecorded in two cohorts (those men sit in the reference group); amount and duration recorded in only six and five cohorts; use assumed stable over up to 26 years of follow-up.

Investigator-assembled cohorts, one of which supplies most deaths; occupational, charity-walk and twin samples; men already using snus at baseline (prevalent use); ever-smokers excluded, which is a design choice that limits the question to snus against no tobacco.
Changes after baseline (starting to smoke, stopping snus) are not tracked; they would push the estimate in opposite directions. The 10-year cap addresses misclassification only in part.

Men with missing body mass index or tobacco information were dropped (5,044); the cause of death is unclassified for 11% of deaths, and the share differs by group (11.5% of deaths in the never-used-tobacco group, 8.8% in the current snus group, 4.9% in the former group; editors' arithmetic), which can bias the cause-specific ratios. Covariates other than age and body mass index are missing for whole cohorts.
Death from a national register is complete and objective for all-cause mortality; cause coding is register-based, with the missing-cause problem recorded under missing data.

No registered protocol is mentioned and no primary estimate is named, but the main analysis is the obvious one and all stated sensitivity analyses are shown; results by cohort and the proportional-hazards test are not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High because of confounding: the main estimate is adjusted for age and body mass index only, in a comparison between men who chose snus and men who used no tobacco, and the one fuller adjustment covers a minority of the data. The association with all-cause death is large in size of data and stable across the sensitivity analyses reported, so it is unlikely to be a chance finding in these cohorts; the study may be cited for the size and consistency of the association between snus-only use and mortality in Swedish men who never smoked, for the pattern by cause, duration and amount, and for the cardiovascular result's fragility; not for the claim that snus causes these deaths, for absolute risks, or for comparison with smoking.

key_findings.finding: 169,103 never-smoking men from eight Swedish cohorts, 2,857,312 person-years, 10,928 deaths. 73.5% had never used tobacco (n = 124,256), 23% currently used snus and no other tobacco (n = 39,156); 4.8% of men in the cohorts that recorded former use had formerly used snus and no other tobacco (n = 5,691 overall).

Exclusive current snus use against never use of tobacco, adjusted for attained age and body mass index: all-cause mortality aHR 1.28 (95% CI 1.20 to 1.35); cardiovascular disease 1.27 (1.15 to 1.41); cancer 1.12 (1.00 to 1.26); other causes 1.37 (1.24 to 1.52). Death counts in the current snus group were 1,410, 443, 332 and 511 (never-used group 9,272, 3,444, 2,660 and 2,098).

Exclusive former snus use against never use: all-cause aHR 1.15 (1.02 to 1.31); cancer 1.26 (1.01 to 1.57); cardiovascular 1.13 (0.91 to 1.41) and other causes 1.14 (0.89 to 1.45), both consistent with no difference.

By duration of use at baseline, all-cause aHR rose from 1.08 (0.88 to 1.32) under 5 years to 1.29 (1.20 to 1.38) at 15 years or more (p for trend 0.001); cardiovascular and other-cause deaths showed the same pattern (p for trend 0.001 each), cancer did not (p for trend 0.11). Few deaths sit in the shorter categories (for example 13 cardiovascular deaths under 5 years).

By weekly amount, all-cause aHR was 1.28 (under 4 cans), 1.17 (4 to 6) and 1.37 (7 or more), p for trend 0.09. The cardiovascular ratio was highest in the lightest group (1.44, 1.18, 1.17; p for trend 0.03), the other-cause ratio highest in the heaviest (1.24, 1.18, 1.65; p for trend 0.001), and cancer showed no pattern (p for trend 0.22).
key_findings.note: The abstract says risks did not increase with weekly amount; the trends by amount differ by cause.

key_findings.finding: Leaving out the Construction Worker Cohort raised the ratios: all-cause 1.42 (1.21 to 1.66), cardiovascular 1.39 (1.05 to 1.84), cancer 1.52 (1.15 to 1.99), other causes 1.34 (0.97 to 1.86).

Capping follow-up at 10 years: all-cause aHR 1.34 (1.21 to 1.48), cancer 1.24 (1.02 to 1.52), other causes 1.57 (1.35 to 1.83), but cardiovascular 1.13 (0.93 to 1.38), no longer distinguishable from no difference. The authors say the cardiovascular result should be read with caution because of this inconsistency.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 4, 10-year block; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Additional adjustment for education, alcohol and physical activity, in the subset of six cohorts that recorded them (the Construction Worker Cohort and the Malmo study left out): all-cause aHR 1.46 (1.22 to 1.75), cardiovascular 1.56 (1.14 to 2.14), cancer 1.51 (1.12 to 2.03), other causes 1.20 (0.83 to 1.72), on 158 snus-group deaths.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 4, additional-adjustment block and footnote b

key_findings.finding: Baseline differences between the groups (Table 2): the current snus group was younger (mean 29 against 38 years), drank more (37.9% in the highest alcohol tertile against 20.2%), and more often had 10 to 12 years of education (52.6% against 38.7%) than men who never used tobacco; body mass index was similar (24.1 against 24.6).

The authors name residual confounding and single baseline measurement of exposure as weaknesses; they note that former snus use was not recorded in two cohorts and that excluding them changed the estimates only marginally; they describe their findings as supporting an association, with public-health relevance 'if causal'.

The authors' suggested explanations (nicotine effects on blood vessels and heart rhythm, nicotine-promoted tumour progression, poorer cancer survival, alcohol-linked self-harm and violence, risk-taking) are hypotheses; none was tested in these data.
Funding came from a university department, Swedish regional authorities and a medical society; funders had no role; no conflicts declared.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods give 383,015 men in the eight cohorts (which reconciles with the 169,103 analysed after the stated exclusions), but the male participants in Table 1 add to 383,025 (editors' arithmetic) and the table's total row prints 383,025.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 1st paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: A 10-man discrepancy that does not touch the analysed sample; worth noting only because the flow cannot be reproduced exactly from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The cause-specific death counts in Table 3 add to 9,722 of the 10,928 deaths (3,970 cardiovascular, 3,074 cancer, 2,678 other), leaving 1,206 deaths (11%) without a classified cause; the share is 11.5% in the never-used-tobacco group, 8.8% in the current snus group and 4.9% in the former group (editors' arithmetic). The Methods define 'other causes' as every death except cardiovascular and cancer, which would include these.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3 and footnote a; Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cause-specific ratios rest on deaths with a known cause, and the different shares of missing causes by group could shift them; the all-cause ratio is not affected. The 'other causes' category as analysed is not the one defined.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the Discussion (1st paragraph) say risks rose with duration but not with weekly amount. Table 3 gives p for trend by amount of 0.09 (all causes), 0.03 (cardiovascular, with the highest ratio in the lightest group), 0.22 (cancer) and 0.001 (other causes); the Discussion (6th paragraph) separately says other-cause deaths show dose-response trends for both amount and duration.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Discussion, 1st and 6th paragraphs; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement about amount holds for all-cause and cancer deaths only. Any claim must state the pattern by cause rather than say there was no gradient with amount.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the mortality risks increased with duration; the cancer row of Table 3 has p for trend 0.11 with ratios of 0.68 to 1.12, and the Results text itself excludes cancer from the statement.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The duration gradient applies to all-cause, cardiovascular and other-cause deaths, not to cancer.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods cite a paper on the Fine and Gray competing-risks model as the reference for the Schoenfeld test of proportional hazards, and the result of that test is not reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph; reference 33
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the proportional-hazards assumption held cannot be judged; given the cardiovascular ratio's drop at 10 years of follow-up, a time-varying hazard ratio is plausible.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods call the eight cohorts population-based, but Table 1 lists a nationwide occupational cohort (construction workers), a charity-walk sample, an employee study and a twin register.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 1st paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Generalisation to all Swedish men is weaker than the wording suggests; the construction workers supply most of the deaths.
